prompt: Which phrase best describes what Redis is?
explanation: Redis (REmote DIctionary Server) keeps data in memory and maps keys to rich data structures (strings, lists, hashes, sets, sorted sets, and more), accessed over the network.

options.text: A relational database that stores tables on disk
An in-memory key-value store that serves rich data structures over the network
A programming language for data processing
A file system optimized for large binary files

prompt: Why is each individual Redis command atomic?
explanation: Redis executes command logic in a single thread, running each command to completion before the next — so a single command can never be observed half-done.

options.text: Because Redis locks every key before writing to it
Because commands are executed one at a time in a single thread, so none can interleave
Because Redis runs every command inside a database transaction with rollback
Because clients coordinate with each other before sending commands

prompt: Which statements about Redis are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Redis persists via RDB/AOF, plays all three roles, and blocks on slow commands (so avoid them). It is NOT entirely single-threaded — only command execution is; it uses extra threads for I/O and background work.

options.text: Redis can persist data to disk with RDB snapshots and/or the AOF
Redis can be used as a cache, a database, and a message broker
Redis is entirely single-threaded and never uses any other threads
A single slow command can block other clients

prompt: Since Redis 8.0 (May 2025), which licensing statement is correct?
explanation: Redis 8.0 added AGPLv3 (an OSI-approved open-source license) alongside the source-available RSALv2 and SSPLv1, making Redis tri-licensed. It did not return to BSD; Valkey is the BSD-licensed fork.

options.text: Redis is closed source with no source available
Redis is available under a choice of AGPLv3 (open source), RSALv2, or SSPLv1
Redis is only under the SSPL and is not open source
Redis returned to the BSD-3-Clause license

prompt: The BSD-licensed fork of Redis 7.2.4, created under the Linux Foundation in 2024, is called ______. (one word)
explanation: Valkey was forked from Redis 7.2.4 after the March 2024 relicense and is governed by the Linux Foundation under the permissive BSD license.

prompt: Match each store to the best short description.
explanation: Redis is a rich in-memory store; Memcached is a plain string cache; a relational database is durable and queryable; Valkey is the open-source fork of Redis.

pairs.right: In-memory data-structure store (cache, DB, and broker)

prompt: What is the default TCP port a Redis server listens on?
explanation: Redis listens on TCP port 6379 by default (5432 is PostgreSQL, 3306 is MySQL).

prompt: How many logical databases does a Redis server expose by default, and how do you switch between them?
explanation: By default there are 16 logical databases (0–15); SELECT changes the current one. They share the same server and config.

options.text: Unlimited databases, switched with USE
16 databases numbered 0–15, switched with SELECT
One database only; there is no switching
8 databases numbered 1–8, switched with SWITCH

prompt: Which statements about redis-cli and RESP are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Command names are case-insensitive and RESP replies are typed; you can pass a command as arguments to redis-cli. But KEYS are case-sensitive.

options.text: Command names are case-insensitive (SET and set both work)
Replies are typed: simple strings, errors, integers, bulk strings, and arrays
Keys are case-insensitive too
You can run a single command like `redis-cli PING` without entering the interactive prompt

prompt: Why are the 16 logical databases a poor choice for isolating separate tenants?
explanation: Logical databases are lightweight namespaces on one server — same memory and config, wiped together by FLUSHALL, and unsupported in Cluster. Use separate instances or key prefixes for isolation.

options.text: They each require a separate license
They share the same server, memory, and configuration, and don't exist in Redis Cluster
They can only hold string values
They are read-only

prompt: The command that deletes every key in the CURRENT database only is ______. (one word)
explanation: FLUSHDB clears the current database; FLUSHALL clears all of them. Both are immediate and irreversible.

prompt: Which command gives you a quick health check that the connection to Redis is working?
explanation: PING returns PONG when the server is reachable and responsive. SAVE, SHUTDOWN, and FLUSHALL all have significant side effects.

options.text: PING (expect PONG)
SAVE
SHUTDOWN
FLUSHALL

prompt: Why should you avoid KEYS on a large production database?
explanation: KEYS scans every key in one command, and since commands run in a single thread, that can block all other clients on a big keyspace. Use SCAN instead.

options.text: It permanently deletes matching keys
It is O(N) over the whole keyspace and can block the server for everyone
It only works on string values
It requires authentication that SCAN does not

prompt: How do you know a SCAN iteration is complete?
explanation: SCAN is cursor-based: you pass the returned cursor back on each call, and iteration is finished when the cursor comes back as 0 (an individual call may return zero keys but a non-zero cursor).

options.text: When it returns an empty array of keys
When the returned cursor is 0
When it returns the same keys twice
SCAN always finishes in a single call

prompt: Which statements about Redis Strings are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Strings are binary-safe up to 512 MB; INCR errors on non-integers; MSET/MGET are multi-key. A plain SET CLEARS the TTL unless you pass KEEPTTL.

options.text: They are binary-safe and can hold up to 512 MB
INCR works only if the current value parses as an integer
A plain SET keeps any existing TTL by default
MSET and MGET operate on several keys in one command

prompt: What does `SET lock:job1 "owner" NX` return if lock:job1 already exists?
explanation: NX means 'only set if the key does not exist.' When the key already exists, SET does nothing and returns (nil).

options.text: OK — it overwrites the value
(nil) — NX refuses to set because the key exists
(error) — NX is not a valid option
(integer) 0

prompt: The command that atomically increases the integer stored at a key by 1 is ______. (one word)
explanation: INCR adds 1 atomically (creating the key as 0 first if needed). Because it's a single command, concurrent increments never lose counts.

prompt: Match each command to what it does.
explanation: EXISTS checks presence, TYPE reports the type, APPEND extends a string (returning its new length), and INCRBYFLOAT does floating-point addition.

pairs.right: Reports whether a key is present
Adds to a string and returns the new length
Adds a floating-point amount to a number

prompt: What is the time complexity of pushing or popping at the ends of a Redis List?
explanation: Lists are linked lists, so operations at the head/tail (LPUSH/RPUSH/LPOP/RPOP) are O(1). Indexed middle access (LINDEX) is O(N).

options.text: O(N) — it walks the whole list
O(1) — constant time, regardless of length
O(log N)
It depends on the value size only

prompt: Which pair of commands implements a FIFO queue?
explanation: For first-in-first-out, push onto the tail (RPUSH) and pop from the head (LPOP). Using the same end (LPUSH+LPOP) gives a LIFO stack.

options.text: LPUSH to add, LPOP to remove
RPUSH to add, LPOP to remove
RPUSH to add, RPOP to remove
SET to add, GET to remove

prompt: Which statements about List commands are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: LTRIM caps a list, BLPOP blocks efficiently, and LMOVE is an atomic pop-and-push. LINDEX is O(N), not O(1).

options.text: LTRIM key 0 99 keeps only the first 100 elements
BLPOP blocks until an element is available or the timeout elapses
LMOVE pops from one list and pushes to another atomically
LINDEX on a huge list is O(1)

prompt: Why prefer BLPOP over an LPOP polling loop for a worker consuming a queue?
explanation: BLPOP blocks until work arrives (up to a timeout), avoiding the wasted CPU and round trips of polling an empty list with LPOP.

options.text: BLPOP can pop multiple keys but LPOP cannot exist
BLPOP waits efficiently for an item instead of repeatedly checking an empty queue
BLPOP guarantees the job is never removed
LPOP is not allowed in production

prompt: To keep a list capped at its most recent 100 items after LPUSH, you run LTRIM key 0 ______. (a number)
explanation: LTRIM key 0 99 keeps indexes 0 through 99 — 100 elements — and discards the rest.

prompt: Which problem does LMOVE (or BLMOVE) into a 'processing' list solve?
explanation: Atomically moving a job from 'pending' to 'processing' means a crashed worker's job still sits in the processing list and can be recovered, rather than being lost as a plain LPOP would.

options.text: It makes list reads O(1)
It prevents losing an in-flight job if the worker crashes before finishing
It compresses the list to save memory
It sorts the list by value

prompt: What does a Redis Hash store under a single key?
explanation: A Hash maps field names to values under one key, which makes it a natural fit for modeling an object like a user or product.

options.text: An ordered list of elements
A set of field-value pairs (a small dictionary)
A sorted collection ranked by score
A single string value only

prompt: What does HSET return?
explanation: HSET returns how many fields were newly created; updates to existing fields still happen but don't add to that count.

options.text: OK
The total number of fields in the hash
The number of NEW fields added (existing ones are updated but not counted)
The value that was overwritten

prompt: Which are genuine advantages of one hash over many separate string keys for an object? Select all that apply.
explanation: Hashes give one-key management, memory savings, and one-shot fetch. Per-field TTLs are NOT the default — they require Redis 7.4+; normally a TTL applies to the whole key.

options.text: You can delete the whole object with a single DEL
Small hashes use less memory via a compact listpack encoding
You can fetch the whole object with one HGETALL
Every field automatically gets its own independent TTL by default

prompt: Why can HGETALL be risky on a very large hash?
explanation: HGETALL doesn't paginate — it returns all fields at once, which is O(N) and can block the server on a huge hash. Use HSCAN to iterate instead.

options.text: It deletes fields as it reads them
It returns every field-value pair in one O(N) blocking command
It only works on hashes with fewer than 10 fields
It requires the hash to be sorted first

prompt: The command that atomically adds an integer to a numeric field of a hash is ______. (one word)
explanation: HINCRBY adds an integer to a hash field atomically (HINCRBYFLOAT does the same for floating-point amounts).

prompt: Which statement about HMSET is correct?
explanation: HMSET is deprecated. Modern HSET accepts multiple field-value pairs, so HSET covers both single and multi-field writes.

options.text: It is the only way to set multiple fields
It is deprecated; HSET now accepts multiple field-value pairs
It sets a field only if it does not exist
It sets a TTL on each field

prompt: Which two properties define a Redis Set?
explanation: A Set is an unordered collection of unique members; adding a duplicate has no effect. (Ordering by score describes a Sorted Set.)

options.text: Ordered by insertion, allows duplicates
Unordered, members are unique (no duplicates)
Ordered by score, members are unique
Ordered alphabetically, allows duplicates

prompt: Which command returns the members present in ALL of the given sets?
explanation: SINTER computes the intersection (members in every set). SUNION is the union, SDIFF is the difference.

options.text: SUNION
SDIFF
SINTER
SMEMBERS

prompt: Which statements about Set commands are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: SADD counts new members, SINTERCARD gives just the intersection size, and SISMEMBER tests membership. SMEMBERS is O(N) and unpaginated — use SSCAN for large sets.

options.text: SADD returns the number of newly added members
SINTERCARD returns the size of an intersection without materializing it
SISMEMBER tests whether a member is in the set
SMEMBERS is a paginated, cheap way to read huge sets

prompt: You want to store the result of a set intersection to reuse it later. Which command helps?
explanation: SINTERSTORE writes the intersection into a destination key so you can reuse it, rather than recomputing with SINTER each time.

options.text: SINTERSTORE
SINTER (it stores automatically)
SCARD
SPOP

prompt: The command that returns the number of members in a set (its cardinality) is ______. (one word)
explanation: SCARD returns the member count of a set in O(1).

prompt: Which is the best use case for a Set rather than a List?
explanation: Sets shine when you need uniqueness and membership tests without ordering — like tags. Queues want a List; rankings want a Sorted Set.

options.text: A FIFO job queue where order matters
The distinct tags on an article, where uniqueness matters and order does not
A ranked leaderboard
The last 100 log lines in order

prompt: What makes a Sorted Set different from a plain Set?
explanation: A Sorted Set keeps unique members, each with a floating-point score, ordered by that score — giving you a live ranking.

options.text: It allows duplicate members
Each member has a numeric score, and members are kept ordered by score
It stores field-value pairs
It is limited to integer values

prompt: Which command reads the three highest-scoring members with their scores?
explanation: REV orders high-to-low so ranks 0–2 are the top three; WITHSCORES includes each score. Without REV you'd get the three LOWEST.

options.text: ZRANGE key 0 2 WITHSCORES
ZRANGE key 0 2 REV WITHSCORES
ZSCORE key 0 2
ZRANK key 0 2

prompt: Which statements about sorted sets are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Core operations are O(log N), ZINCRBY is atomic, and scoring by timestamp enables time-range queries. Members are unique — a member has exactly one score.

options.text: ZADD and ZSCORE are O(log N)
ZINCRBY atomically changes a member's score
The score can be used as a timestamp for range queries
Members can appear multiple times with different scores

prompt: You need a priority queue where workers take the highest-priority job first. Which command fits?
explanation: Use the score as priority; ZPOPMAX removes and returns the highest-scored member (BZPOPMAX blocks until one is available).

options.text: ZRANK
ZPOPMAX (or blocking BZPOPMAX)
ZSCORE
ZCARD

prompt: To read members whose score falls in a range (e.g. a time window), use Z________ key min max. (complete the command name)
explanation: ZRANGEBYSCORE returns members within a [min, max] score range (the modern equivalent is ZRANGE key min max BYSCORE).

prompt: Match each command to what it returns.
explanation: ZSCORE gives the score, ZREVRANK the descending rank, ZINCRBY the updated score, and ZCARD the member count.

pairs.right: A member's position counting from the top
The member's new score after adding to it

prompt: What does `TTL key` return for a key that exists but has no expiry set?
explanation: TTL returns -1 when the key exists but has no expiry, and -2 when the key does not exist. A positive number is the seconds remaining.

options.text: (nil)

prompt: How does Redis expire keys? Select all that apply.
explanation: Expiration is passive plus active (eventual, not a precise timer), but reads never return an expired value — it's logically gone the moment it expires.

options.text: Passively — an expired key is removed when a client next accesses it
Actively — a background cycle samples keys with TTLs and removes expired ones
With a precise per-key timer that fires the exact millisecond the TTL hits zero
A read will never return a value that has already expired

prompt: You run `SET k "v" EX 100`, then later `SET k "v2"`. What is the TTL of k afterward?
explanation: A full-replacement SET clears any existing TTL. To keep it you'd use SET k "v2" KEEPTTL or re-apply EXPIRE.

options.text: Still around 100 seconds
-1 (the TTL was cleared by the plain SET)
-2 (the key was deleted)
200 seconds

prompt: How is expiration different from eviction?
explanation: A TTL is a deadline you set on one key; eviction is triggered by hitting maxmemory and can remove keys (even ones without TTLs) according to the configured policy.

options.text: They are two names for the same thing
Expiration removes a key when its own TTL is due; eviction removes keys under memory pressure per a policy
Expiration only happens in Redis Cluster; eviction only on a single node
Eviction applies only to keys that have a TTL

prompt: The command that removes a key's TTL so it stops expiring is ______. (one word)
explanation: PERSIST removes the expiry, leaving the key in place until it is explicitly deleted (TTL then returns -1).

prompt: Which single command sets a value AND a 60-second expiry atomically?
explanation: SET with the EX option sets the value and the relative expiry in one atomic command, avoiding a window where the key exists without a TTL.

options.text: SET key value EX 60
SET key value; EXPIRE key 60 (two commands)
TTL key 60
PERSIST key 60

prompt: Which statement about Redis Bitmaps is correct?
explanation: Bitmap commands (SETBIT, GETBIT, BITCOUNT, BITOP) treat a String as an array of bits — there is no separate 'bitmap' type.

options.text: They are a distinct data type separate from strings
They are bit-level operations performed on ordinary String values
They can only store 64 bits
They automatically compress sparse data

prompt: What does a HyperLogLog give you?
explanation: A HyperLogLog estimates cardinality (distinct count) in a fixed ~12 KB with about 0.81% error; it does not store or return the individual elements.

options.text: An exact count and the ability to list all members
An approximate count of distinct elements using fixed, tiny memory
A sorted list of the most frequent elements
A way to store and retrieve large blobs

prompt: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: PFADD/PFCOUNT work as described, HLL memory is near-constant, and BITOP combines bitmaps. You canNOT list a HyperLogLog's members.

options.text: PFADD adds elements to a HyperLogLog; PFCOUNT returns the estimated distinct count
A HyperLogLog uses roughly the same memory whether it holds thousands or billions of elements
You can read individual elements back out of a HyperLogLog
BITOP can combine two bitmaps with AND/OR/XOR/NOT

prompt: For which task is a HyperLogLog the WRONG choice?
explanation: HyperLogLog is approximate (~0.81% error) and can't list members, so it's unsuitable for exact, auditable counts like billing — use a Set or a database.

options.text: Reporting roughly how many unique visitors a huge site had today
Billing each customer for the exact number of distinct API callers, auditable
Estimating distinct search terms across billions of queries
Rolling daily unique estimates up into a monthly total with PFMERGE

prompt: The command that counts the number of set (1) bits in a bitmap is ______. (one word)
explanation: BITCOUNT counts the 1-bits, optionally within a byte (or BIT) range.

prompt: When is a bitmap a poor fit for tracking boolean state per item?
explanation: A bitmap's size is driven by the highest offset you set, so large, sparse IDs waste huge amounts of space. Bitmaps shine with dense integer IDs.

options.text: When item IDs are dense small integers
When item IDs are large and sparse (e.g. random 64-bit numbers)
When you need to count set bits
When you want to combine two days with BITOP

prompt: What is the delivery model of Redis Pub/Sub?
explanation: Pub/Sub delivers messages only to clients subscribed at publish time and stores nothing — so a subscriber that isn't listening misses the message permanently.

options.text: At-least-once, with messages persisted until acknowledged
Fire-and-forget / at-most-once — messages aren't stored
Exactly-once, guaranteed
Ordered and durable, like a log

prompt: What does the integer returned by PUBLISH mean?
explanation: PUBLISH returns how many subscribers received the message. It says nothing about whether they successfully processed it.

options.text: The number of clients that received the message
The number of messages stored for later delivery
Confirmation that every subscriber processed the message
The channel's total message count

prompt: Which are true about Pub/Sub? Select all that apply.
explanation: No history, pattern subscriptions, and the RESP2 subscribed-connection restriction are all true. Pub/Sub does NOT persist or replay messages.

options.text: A subscriber that connects later cannot see past messages
PSUBSCRIBE subscribes to channels by glob pattern
Messages are written to disk and can be replayed
On a RESP2 connection in subscribe mode, you can only run (un)subscribe commands

prompt: You must not lose 'process this payment' messages even if the worker briefly restarts. What should you use?
explanation: Streams persist entries and support at-least-once delivery via consumer groups and XACK, so a restarting worker can catch up — Pub/Sub would drop messages sent while it was down.

options.text: Pub/Sub with PSUBSCRIBE
Streams with consumer groups and acknowledgements
Pub/Sub on a dedicated connection
Sharded Pub/Sub

prompt: The Cluster-friendly variant of PUBLISH that keeps a channel on the shard that owns it is ______. (one word)
explanation: Sharded Pub/Sub (SPUBLISH/SSUBSCRIBE, added in Redis 7.0) scopes a channel to one shard so publishing scales on Cluster.

prompt: Why is cache invalidation over Pub/Sub often paired with TTLs?
explanation: Because a briefly-disconnected server can miss the invalidation broadcast, a TTL guarantees the stale entry eventually expires anyway — a safety net for the at-most-once delivery.

options.text: TTLs make Pub/Sub messages persistent
A server that misses the invalidation message will still drop the stale value when its TTL expires
Pub/Sub requires a TTL to function
TTLs increase PUBLISH throughput

prompt: How does a Stream differ from Pub/Sub?
explanation: Streams are an append-only, persistent log — entries stay and can be re-read by ID. Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget with no history.

options.text: A Stream persists its entries so they can be replayed by ID; Pub/Sub stores nothing
A Stream delivers to every subscriber; Pub/Sub delivers to one
A Stream cannot have more than one consumer
There is no real difference

prompt: What does passing `*` as the ID to XADD do?
explanation: `*` asks Redis to generate the next ID (a millisecond timestamp plus a sequence number), keeping the stream strictly ordered.

options.text: Deletes the oldest entry
Tells Redis to auto-generate the next (increasing) entry ID
Reads all entries
Acknowledges the entry

prompt: Which statements about consumer groups are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Consumer groups split work, track unacked entries in the PEL, and clear them with XACK. XACK does NOT delete the entry from the stream itself — trimming (MAXLEN/XTRIM) does that.

options.text: Each entry is delivered to one consumer in the group, not all of them
An unacknowledged entry stays in the Pending Entries List (PEL)
XACK removes an entry from the PEL
Entries are automatically deleted from the stream once acknowledged

prompt: A consumer reads an entry with XREADGROUP but crashes before acknowledging it. What happens?
explanation: Because delivery is at-least-once, the unacknowledged entry remains pending and another consumer can claim and finish it — nothing is silently lost.

options.text: The entry is lost permanently
The entry stays in the PEL and can be reclaimed by another consumer via XCLAIM/XAUTOCLAIM
The whole stream is rolled back
The entry is delivered to every other consumer immediately

prompt: The command a consumer runs to acknowledge that it finished processing a stream entry is ______. (one word)
explanation: XACK marks an entry as processed and removes it from the group's Pending Entries List.

prompt: How do you keep a busy stream from consuming memory without bound?
explanation: Streams persist, so you must bound them explicitly with MAXLEN (the ~ makes trimming approximate and cheaper) or XTRIM. XACK only clears the PEL, not the log.

options.text: It trims itself automatically
Cap it with MAXLEN on XADD (e.g. MAXLEN ~ 10000) or trim with XTRIM
Call XACK on every entry
Streams never use memory

prompt: What does MULTI/EXEC guarantee about the queued commands?
explanation: EXEC runs the queued commands one after another with no interleaving from other clients — isolation. It does not provide rollback.

options.text: They roll back entirely if any command fails
They run as one unit with no other client's commands interleaving
They run in parallel across threads
They are retried automatically on failure

prompt: During EXEC, one queued command errors because it targets the wrong type. What happens to the other commands?
explanation: A run-time error in one command does not undo the others; Redis transactions have no rollback. Only a queuing-time error (before EXEC) aborts the whole transaction.

options.text: They are all rolled back
They still execute — Redis has no rollback
EXEC refuses to run any command
They are queued again for a retry

prompt: Which statements about WATCH are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: WATCH is optimistic (no lock is held); it aborts EXEC with (nil) if a watched key changed, signaling a retry. It does NOT take an exclusive lock.

options.text: It provides optimistic locking (check-and-set)
If a watched key changes before EXEC, EXEC returns (nil)
It holds an exclusive lock on the key until EXEC
A (nil) result from EXEC means you should retry

prompt: Why can't you read a value inside MULTI and branch on it before EXEC?
explanation: Commands between MULTI and EXEC are only queued (they reply QUEUED), so their results aren't available to branch on. Use WATCH for check-and-set, or a Lua script to compute before writing.

options.text: Reads are forbidden inside transactions
Queued commands don't return their values until EXEC runs them
MULTI encrypts all replies
Branching requires Redis Cluster

prompt: The command that abandons a queued transaction without executing anything is ______. (one word)
explanation: DISCARD throws away the queued commands and ends the transaction; nothing runs.

prompt: For atomic read-compute-write logic that needs to branch before writing, what is often a better fit than MULTI/EXEC?
explanation: A Lua script (or Redis Function) executes atomically as one uninterruptible unit and can read, decide, and write — cleaner than a transaction for conditional logic.

options.text: Pipelining
A Lua script or Redis Function (runs atomically and can make decisions)
Running the commands one at a time with no coordination
SUBSCRIBE

prompt: In `EVAL script numkeys ...`, what does numkeys tell Redis?
explanation: numkeys splits the arguments: the first numkeys of them are key names (KEYS[1..]), and the remainder are ARGV. Passing keys explicitly is also what lets Cluster route correctly.

options.text: How many times to run the script
How many of the following arguments are keys (populating KEYS), with the rest going to ARGV
The maximum runtime in milliseconds
The number of return values

prompt: Why must Lua scripts be kept short and fast?
explanation: A script's atomicity comes from monopolizing the one command thread, so a long-running script freezes every other client until it finishes.

options.text: Because Lua is a slow language
Because a script runs atomically on the single command thread, blocking all other clients while it runs
Because scripts can only use 1 KB of memory
Because EVAL charges per second

prompt: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Scripts are atomic, EVALSHA uses the cached SHA-1, and Functions are persisted/replicated. EVAL scripts are only an ephemeral cache — they are NOT stored with the dataset.

options.text: A Lua script executes atomically — no other command interleaves
EVALSHA runs a script cached by its SHA-1 hash
Redis Functions are persisted with the dataset and replicated
EVAL scripts are permanently stored in RDB/AOF like data

prompt: What is a key advantage of Redis Functions over EVAL scripts?
explanation: Functions (Redis 7.0+) are first-class: named, managed as a library, and stored with the dataset (RDB/AOF) and replicated — unlike the ephemeral script cache behind EVAL.

options.text: They run faster because they skip atomicity
They are named, loaded as a library, and persisted/replicated with the data
They can block the server without consequences
They do not need keys or arguments

prompt: Inside a Lua script, you invoke a Redis command with redis.____('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]). (the function name that raises on error)
explanation: redis.call runs a command and raises an error (aborting the script) if it fails; redis.pcall instead returns the error as a value.

prompt: Why should a script receive the keys it touches through KEYS rather than hard-coding them?
explanation: Declaring keys via KEYS lets Redis (and Cluster) know which keys the script operates on, which is necessary to route the command to the right shard.

options.text: It makes the script run twice as fast
So Redis knows which keys are accessed, which is required for correct routing in Redis Cluster
Hard-coded keys are not allowed in Lua
It reduces the SHA-1 length

prompt: What is the main risk of RDB (snapshot) persistence?
explanation: RDB captures the dataset at points in time; between snapshots, recent writes exist only in memory and are lost if Redis crashes.

options.text: It makes restarts extremely slow
On a crash you lose everything written since the last snapshot
It cannot be used for backups
It logs every command, so files grow forever

prompt: What is the default appendfsync policy, and roughly how much data can it lose?
explanation: The default appendfsync is everysec: it flushes to disk about once per second, so a crash risks roughly the last second of writes — a balance of durability and speed.

options.text: always — essentially no loss
everysec — up to about one second
no — potentially many seconds
AOF has no fsync policy

prompt: Which statements about Redis persistence are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: BGSAVE is a background fork, AOF replays commands, and both can be enabled together. AOF restarts are usually SLOWER than RDB because it replays commands rather than loading a snapshot.

options.text: BGSAVE forks a background process so the server keeps serving during the snapshot
AOF replays logged write commands on restart to rebuild the data
You can enable both RDB and AOF at the same time
AOF always restarts faster than RDB

prompt: Which option gives effectively zero data loss on a crash (at the cost of speed)?
explanation: appendfsync always flushes every write to disk before acknowledging, giving near-zero loss — but every write waits on disk, so it's the slowest option.

options.text: RDB with frequent save rules
AOF with appendfsync always
AOF with appendfsync no
